Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Vignette:
The typhoon struck during a Tuesday evening when Linh was cataloguing donated manuscripts in the library’s basement archives. When the emergency generators died, the room plunged into absolute darkness. She was certain that the sudden, suffocating silence that followed when the backup pumps failed meant the water was rising unchecked. Hours later, emergency responders finally cut through the steel door. Their grim expressions and urgent, clipped commands imprinted themselves on her mind as they hauled her onto a narrow cot while the floodwater lapped at her knees. Linh had spent years rebuilding a routine, yet the past refused to stay buried. Whenever the morning shift ends, the silence in the public library reading room drops over her like a physical weight. She tracks every shadow along the stacks, eyes constantly scanning the aisles for structural shifts or flickering lights. What frightened her most was the way the quiet no longer felt empty, but like a held breath. She always positions her reference desk near the heavy oak partition in the center of the room, her back to the wall, watching the aisles. When a patron approaches from an angle she cannot see, her breath catches, but she forces her hands to stay steady over the checkout terminal. A dropped stack of books, the damp smell of the return cart, or a sudden draft near the windows can instantly pull her back to the concrete steps. When it happens, the grief arrives as a heavy wave that leaves her gripping the edge of the desk until her knuckles whiten. She steps away from the room, focusing on the temperature of the floorboards until her senses feel distant, as if she is watching herself through thick glass. It is a practiced escape, a way to steady her hands long enough to shelve another box. She has also stopped running. The last time she tried to complete a morning jog, the burning in her lungs and the rhythm of her feet triggered a terror so sharp she had to stop under a streetlamp. Now, she avoids the gym entirely. Afternoons are harder. Whenever the evening cleaning crew turns off the main switches, leaving only the red glow of exit signs, she packs her bag quickly. The dark is not merely an absence of light to her; it is the same blackness that swallowed the archive room. She walks home with her keys between her fingers, noting the positions of every vehicle along the curb, taking the stairs instead of the elevator. Linh finally walked into the community clinic last month because her husband noticed she was flinching when she poured her coffee, and because the quiet in their own house had begun to echo. She does not want to keep blanking out or steering clear of every dim corridor. What she hopes for is simple: to sit in the reading room without feeling the water rising, and to let the silence be just silence.
